reference.source: Auerbach's Wilderness Medicine / Bove and Davis' Diving Medicine
clinicalPearls: Painful, involuntary muscle spasms occurring during or after strenuous exertion in the heat, typically in the heavily worked large muscle groups of the legs, arms, and abdomen
Classically affects unacclimatised individuals who sweat profusely and replace losses with water alone, leading to a sodium-depletion state
Core temperature and mental status are normal, distinguishing cramps from more serious heat illness
The mechanism is best understood as a sodium (salt) deficit rather than simple dehydration or a lack of potassium, calcium, or magnesium
Treatment is rest in a cool place and replacement of both salt and fluid, using oral electrolyte solutions or, in severe cases, intravenous saline
Plain water without added electrolyte can worsen the sodium deficit and prolong symptoms
Acclimatisation and adequate dietary salt greatly reduce recurrence in those working or exercising in the heat
reference.pathophysiology: Heat cramps result from selective loss of sodium and chloride in sweat during heavy exertion, compounded when fluid losses are replaced with water that dilutes the remaining extracellular sodium. The relative sodium depletion and altered fluid balance at the neuromuscular junction of fatigued, heavily used muscles provoke sustained, painful contraction. Because overall thermoregulation is preserved, the core temperature and sensorium stay normal, marking this as a comparatively benign point on the spectrum of heat illness, though it may accompany or precede heat exhaustion.
additionalDifferentials: Ordinary exercise-associated muscle cramp from fatigue
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment with normal core temperature and mentation
Serum sodium and chloride to confirm salt depletion and exclude hyponatraemia
Other electrolytes (potassium, calcium, magnesium) to exclude alternative causes
Creatine kinase where rhabdomyolysis is suspected
Renal function and urinalysis in severe or prolonged cases
redFlags: Marked hyperthermia or altered mental status suggesting heat stroke rather than simple cramps
Very dark urine, severe muscle pain, or weakness suggesting rhabdomyolysis
Documented hyponatraemia, which changes fluid management entirely
Failure to settle with rest and salt/fluid replacement
reference.prognosis: Heat cramps are self-limiting and resolve quickly with rest and combined salt and fluid replacement; recurrence is common without acclimatisation and adequate sodium intake but long-term sequelae are not expected.
pitfalls: Attributing cramps to potassium, calcium, or magnesium deficiency and missing the underlying sodium deficit
Replacing losses with plain water and worsening the picture
Failing to recognise coexisting heat exhaustion
Overlooking exertional hyponatraemia before giving hypotonic fluids
management: Rest the affected muscles in a cool environment away from ongoing heat stress
Replace both salt and fluid together using an oral electrolyte solution, or intravenous saline in severe cases
Avoid plain water alone, which dilutes extracellular sodium and prolongs the cramps
Apply gentle stretching and passive movement to the cramping muscle groups
Check serum sodium and chloride to confirm salt depletion and exclude hyponatraemia
Prevent recurrence through acclimatisation and adequate dietary and electrolyte salt intake before heavy exertion
